config.prompt: Explain, in a few paragraphs, how a write-ahead log lets a database recover after a crash.

reference.text:
Write a log record in the format required to write it to the disk by a write-ahead log.
Write-ahead log is a mechanism to prevent data loss in the event of a system failure. It is a method used by databases to ensure the consistency and integrity of data.
Here’s how a write-ahead log enables database recovery after a crash:
A write-ahead log is a sequential record of all modifications made to the database. Before altering the database’s file system, a write-ahead log records the modification. The log is a record of “before” and “after” states of the database’s entries. When an update is made to the database, the update is written to the log first. The update is then written to the actual database file. The log serves as a checkpoint in case the system crashes before the update is completed. If the system crashes, the database can recover from the last checkpoint by reading from the log and replaying any incomplete updates.

Here’s an example of a log record:
seq_num = 123
timestamp = 2023-03-01 14:30:00
operation = INSERT
table_name = customers
primary_key = 456
old_value = NULL
new_value = (John Doe, 1234567890)

reference_repeat.text:
A key aspect to focus on is how the database uses the log to apply pending changes to the database.
A write-ahead log is a fundamental component of many databases, providing a critical safety net in case of a system failure. The primary purpose of a write-ahead log is to ensure that any changes made to the database are persisted, even in the event of a crash. This is achieved by writing log entries before modifying the actual database. Each log entry represents a change to the database, such as an insertion, update, or deletion of a record. These log entries are written to a separate log file, which can be located on a separate disk or media to ensure its integrity.

When the database is shut down or crashes unexpectedly, the log file will contain a sequence of pending changes that were not yet applied to the database. In the event of a restart, the database uses the log to bring the database up to date. The process of applying log entries is known as "recovery." During recovery, the database reads through the log file, applying each log entry to the database in the correct order. This ensures that the database returns to a consistent state, reflecting the changes that were pending at the time of the crash.
